title: Walking meditation
hook: slow walking, feeling each step, as taught in Buddhist monasteries

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diogenes stood up and walked, and the Latin said it is solved by walking. Your line was walk it out. Did your question walk with you? Day one hundred thirty.

Yesterday's walk was for thinking. Today's walk is for not thinking. Picture a monastery courtyard in Thailand or Myanmar, early morning. A monk walks a straight path of maybe twenty paces. At the end, he stops, turns slowly, and walks back. Then again. And again. For an hour. He isn't going anywhere, and that's the point. Most of our walking is getting from here to there: to the car, to the fridge, to the next thing, with the mind already arrived. This kind of walking has nowhere to arrive. Every step is the whole trip. Today's practice is walking meditation.
screen: `A MONK ON A SHORT PATH.` → `TURN, AND WALK BACK.` → `NOWHERE TO ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: In the Pali texts, the word for it is cankama, walking up and down, and the walking path itself carries the same name. Early Buddhist monasteries had paths built for it. And the Buddha, in one short teaching from the book of fives, lists five benefits of walking meditation. It gives you endurance for journeys. It gives you endurance for effort. It's good for health. It helps digestion. And the calm you find while walking lasts a long time. That last one matters: a calm that can walk is a calm you can take into the day. The practice looks different from school to school. In Burmese vipassana, taught by teachers like Mahasi Sayadaw, you break each step into parts and note them silently: lifting, moving, placing. In Zen, kinhin is walking meditation between long sits, slow, hands held at the chest, one half step to each breath. In the twentieth century, the Vietnamese Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh taught walking meditation to huge crowds, often outdoors, and made it one of the best-known Buddhist practices in the West. The common thread is simple. Feel the foot. Feel the weight shift. Let the next step be the only step. When your mind drifts to the grocery list, and it will, you notice, and come back to the sole of your foot. It's the same move as watching the breath, done with legs.
screen: `CANKAMA: WALKING UP AND DOWN.` · `FIVE BENEFITS OF WALKING.` · `LIFTING, MOVING, PLACING.` · `FEEL THE FOOT, COME BACK.` · then, large: `THIS STEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ten slow steps. If you can stand, stand. If not, do it with your feet on the floor where you sit. Shift your weight into one foot. Lift the other. Move it forward. Place it. Feel the heel, then the whole sole, take the weight. Say inside: this step. Then the next. Ten steps, slower than feels normal. If you run out of room, turn slowly and come back. The bell holds the time.
Walking meditation. Slow steps on a short path, feeling each one, taught in Buddhist monasteries for centuries. Today's word.
Your line: this step. Today, take the ten steps from one room to the next as a walking meditation. Feel the floor. Say your line once. Day one hundred thirty.

howItsDone: In many Buddhist monasteries, monks and visitors alternate sitting meditation with walking meditation on a short straight path, walking slowly and turning at each end.

original.note: Pali, cankama (caṅkama): walking up and down; the word also names the walking path itself.

trapdoor: what you thought: a slow, spiritual stroll.
what it means: attention on each step, coming back to the foot whenever the mind wanders.
what a scholar hears: cankama, praised in the Anguttara Nikaya's book of fives; early monasteries built walking paths for it.
